newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish banking merger hopes deflated - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Swedish banking merger hopes deflated - analysts.

text.p: The merger and takeover rally fuelling Swedish banking shares could soon be over as restructuring is not likely to be as revolutionary as investors had hoped, analysts said on Thursday.

"There is too much merger speculation in share prices at the moment," said Fredrik Myre'n, analyst at HSBC James Capel in Stockholm, adding that not that many restructuring moves are likely to appear.
After surging 9.8 percent in the past two months, outperforming a general index jump of 8.9 percent, shares were so expensive that a string of bids was unlikely, analysts said.
Takeover and mergers were also so complicated and expensive that there would not be an abundance of them, they said.
Furthermore, large sector restructuring could be detrimental for banks as they are likely to lose customers and provide more room for niche banks, some analysts argued.
With all these obstacles to a wave of mergers, analysts said share prices were likely to level out or fall back.
"Mergers are discounted in current share prices and if no deals appear, prices will drop," a Stockholm-based analyst said.

And even if the hoped for mega deal between two of Sweden's four leading banks Handelsbanken, S-E-Banken, Nordbanken and Swedbank took place, share prices were not certain to leap as stocks were fully valued at the moment, analysts said.
The only deals likely to take place, according to analysts, involved mortgage institute Stadshypotek which had already been bid for, and banking group Foreningsbanken.
On Monday this week, the finance ministry received bids for its 34 percent stake in Stadshypotek but most analysts expected the offers to encompass all the institute's shares.
Regarding Foreningsbanken, analysts say it was just a matter of time before Swedbank swallowed it up.

Swedbank bought a 4.98 percent stake in the bank on June 25 this year and indicated it was interested in more, but Swedbank had met tough resistance from Foreningsbanken's management and from farmer's association LRF, which holds a 20 percent stake in the bank.
"Swedbank and Foreningsbanken are a good fit and a merger would mean that they could close many branch offices," Myre'n at HSBC James Capel said.
Regarding the big four, analysts are talking about merger obstacles rather than merger possibilities.
"Although the streamlining potential would be the largest in a merger between S-E-Banken and Handelsbanken, that deal is very unlikely as the banks are too different," an analyst said.
While Handelsbanken had a flat structure and focuses on cost awareness, S-E-banken had more of a hierarchy and was more of a risk taker, analysts said.
Also, Handelsbanken's employees owned about 9.9 percent of the bank's equity and were unlikely to approve a bid that could risk their jobs.
Deals between the other banks could not be excluded, but analysts pointed to high share prices and other obstacles.
"The costs of integrating IT systems are very large," a Stockholm analyst said. "Reducing staff is also very costly and such a decision will be fought by unions."
Another analyst cautioned, "What you save in costs, you lose in income as you lose customers and create more room for niche banks."
